Prayer, self-control and protection from sin (verses 1–4)

The more we value God's gracious presence, the more earnestly we will seek him in prayer.

David asked God to come quickly.

Our prayers become acceptable to him through the sacrifice and intercession of Jesus Christ, just as the daily sacrifices and burning of incense were acceptable under the former covenant.

Prayer is a spiritual sacrifice in which we offer our souls and best affections to God.

Faithful people know the danger of sins committed with the tongue.

When enemies provoke us, we may speak rashly and do wrong.

Because we live in a fallen world and have sinful hearts, we need grace to keep us from being enticed or driven into evil.

Sinners imagine that sin offers them delicious food.

But its pleasures quickly turn bitter.

Those who understand this pray that the Lord will remove such enticements and turn their hearts against them.

God's people pray against the pleasures of sin.

Welcoming correction and seeking rescue (verses 5–10)

We should receive our heavenly Father's correction and welcome loving rebuke from fellow believers.

It will not break my head if it helps to break my hard heart.

We should respond to such correction gratefully.

Those who formerly ignored God's word may welcome it eagerly once suffering has opened their ears to instruction.

When the world tastes bitter, God's word tastes sweet.

We should pray for deliverance from Satan's traps and from the schemes of people devoted to wrongdoing.

Lord, let our inadequate prayers express the fact that you alone are our hope and confidence.

Prepare us for faithful prayer through your grace.

Clothe us in Christ's righteousness and plant the Holy Spirit's gifts within our hearts.

[Ps.141.1-Ps.141.4]
Chapter 141
Chapter Outline
David prays for God's acceptance and assistance. | (1-4) |
That God would appear for his rescue. | (5-10) |
Verses 1-4
Make haste unto me. Those that know how to value God's gracious presence, will be the more fervent in their prayers. When presented through the sacrifice and intercession of the Saviour, they will be as acceptable to God as the daily sacrifices and burnings of incense were of old. Prayer is a spiritual sacrifice, it is the offering up the soul and its best affections. Good men know the evil of tongue sins. When enemies are provoking, we are in danger of speaking unadvisedly. While we live in an evil world, and have such evil hearts, we have need to pray that we may neither be drawn nor driven to do any thing sinful. Sinners pretend to find dainties in sin; but those that consider how soon sin will turn into bitterness, will dread such dainties, and pray to God to take them out of their sight, and by his grace to turn their hearts against them. Good men pray against the sweets of sin.
[Ps.141.5-Ps.141.10]
Verses 5-10
We should be ready to welcome the rebuke of our heavenly Father, and also the reproof of our brethren. It shall not break my head, if it may but help to break my heart: we must show that we take it kindly. Those who slighted the word of God before, will be glad of it when in affliction, for that opens the ear to instruction. When the world is bitter, the word is sweet. Let us lift our prayer unto God. Let us entreat him to rescue us from the snares of Satan, and of all the workers of iniquity. In language like this psalm, O Lord, would we entreat that our poor prayers should set forth our only hope, our only dependence on thee. Grant us thy grace, that we may be prepared for this employment, being clothed with thy righteousness, and having all the gifts of thy Spirit planted in our hearts.

modern_osis:
Original heading

David's comfort in prayer.

Bringing every trouble before God

No danger or sorrow is so severe that a believer cannot receive comfort by praying in faith.

We are often tempted to examine our troubles repeatedly in our own minds, only making them appear worse.

That accomplishes little.

How much better to lay those troubles before the Lord, casting our cares upon the One who cares for us!

We should never allow ourselves to complain inwardly or to other people in a way that we would be ashamed to bring before God.

When our spirits are overwhelmed and discouraged, when enemies have placed traps along the way we are trying to obey, we can remember that the Lord knows our path.

Those who sincerely receive the Lord as their God find him completely sufficient as their Refuge and their Portion.

Everything else is a refuge of lies and an inheritance of no value.

David therefore prayed earnestly.

The psalm also describes the spiritual condition of believers struggling with doubt and fear.

They should ask the Lord to set their souls free so that they can run eagerly in the way of his commandments.

God delivered David from enemies stronger than himself and treated him generously.

He likewise raised the crucified Redeemer to the throne of glory and made him Head over all things for the benefit of his church.

A sinner awakened to guilt cries for help and is eventually brought to praise God among the redeemed.

All genuine believers will finally be delivered from this evil world, sin and death, and will praise their Savior forever.
classic_reading:
[Ps.142.1]
Chapter 142
David's comfort in prayer.
--There can be no situation so distressing or dangerous, in which faith will not get comfort from God by prayer. We are apt to show our troubles too much to ourselves, poring upon them, which does us no service; whereas, by showing them to God, we might cast the cares upon him who careth for us, and thereby ease ourselves. Nor should we allow any complaint to ourselves or others, which we cannot make to God. When our spirits are overwhelmed by distress, and filled with discouragement; when we see snares laid for us on every side, while we walk in his way, we may reflect with comfort that the Lord knoweth our path. Those who in sincerity take the Lord for their God, find him all-sufficient, as a Refuge, and as a Portion: every thing else is a refuge of lies, and a portion of no value. In this situation David prayed earnestly to God. We may apply it spiritually; the souls of believers are often straitened by doubts and fears. And it is then their duty and interest to beg of God to set them at liberty, that they may run the way of his commandments. Thus the Lord delivered David from his powerful persecutors, and dealt bountifully with him. Thus he raised the crucified Redeemer to the throne of glory, and made him Head over all things for his church. Thus the convinced sinner cries for help, and is brought to praise the Lord in the company of his redeemed people; and thus all believers will at length be delivered from this evil world, from sin and death, and praise their Saviour for ever.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid complains of his enemies and distresses.1–6He prays for comfort, guidance, and deliverance.7–12
Pleading God's righteousness rather than our merit (verses 1–6)

We possess no righteousness of our own that would justify our prayers.

We must therefore appeal to God's righteousness and the promises he has freely given us.

David asked for the forgiveness of sin before asking to be relieved from suffering.

He relied on mercy alone for pardon.

He confessed the heaviness of his heart under trouble.

But he also looked back to remember God's earlier deliverances—those granted to Israel and those he had personally experienced.

He looked around at God's works in creation.

The more we consider God's power, the less we will fear the power or threats of other people.

He lifted his thoughts toward God and longed earnestly for his favor.

This is the best response when our spirits are overwhelmed.

The believer never forgets that even the best acts remain mixed with sin.

Meditation and prayer help restore our souls.

A sorrowing heart reaches toward God like an infant stretching out its hands to a tender mother, and longs for consolation like dry earth thirsting for rain.

Asking to know and do God's will (verses 7–12)

David prayed for God's favor and for the assurance that he enjoyed it.

He knew how miserable he would be if the Lord withdrew his consoling presence.

But the night of affliction will eventually end in a morning of comfort and praise.

He asked to understand God's will.

Henry calls this the first work of the Spirit.

The faithful person does not ask merely which road is easiest or most pleasant.

The right road matters more than the comfortable road.

Lord, do not only reveal your will to me; teach me how to carry it out.

Those who know the Lord as their God have the Holy Spirit as their Guide.

David also asked for renewed life and strength to obey.

Above all, we should ask for our sins to be destroyed, since they are our most dangerous enemies, so that we can serve the Lord faithfully.
classic_reading:
[Ps.143.1-Ps.143.6]
Chapter 143
Chapter Outline
David complains of his enemies and distresses. | (1-6) |
He prays for comfort, guidance, and deliverance. | (7-12) |
Verses 1-6
We have no righteousness of our own to plead, therefore must plead God's righteousness, and the word of promise which he has freely given us, and caused us to hope in. David, before he prays for the removal of his trouble, prays for the pardon of his sin, and depends upon mercy alone for it. He bemoans the weight upon his mind from outward troubles. But he looks back, and remembers God's former appearance for his afflicted people, and for him in particular. He looks round, and notices the works of God. The more we consider the power of God, the less we shall fear the face or force of man. He looks up with earnest desires towards God and his favour. This is the best course we can take, when our spirits are overwhelmed. The believer will not forget, that in his best actions he is a sinner. Meditation and prayer will recover us from distresses; and then the mourning soul strives to return to the Lord as the infant stretches out its hands to the indulgent mother, and thirsts for his consolations as the parched ground for refreshing rain.
[Ps.143.7-Ps.143.12]
Verses 7-12
David prays that God would be well pleased with him, and let him know that he was so. He pleads the wretchedness of his case, if God withdrew from him. But the night of distress and discouragement shall end in a morning of consolation and praise. He prays that he might be enlightened with the knowledge of God's will; and this is the first work of the Spirit. A good man does not ask the way in which is the most pleasant walking, but what is the right way. Not only show me what thy will is, but teach me how to do it. Those who have the Lord for their God, have his Spirit for their Guide; they are led by the Spirit. He prays that he might be enlivened to do God's will. But we should especially seek the destruction of our sins, our worst enemies, that we may be devotedly God's servants.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid acknowledges the great goodness of God, and prays for help.1–8He prays for the prosperity of his kingdom.9–15
Remembering mercy and asking for more (verses 1–8)

When people become skilled and successful despite having few natural advantages, they should be especially aware that God has been their Teacher.

The greatest victory he gives is victory over one's own spirit, through self-control.

A prayer for further help should begin with thanksgiving for the mercy already received.

God exercised special power by moving Israel's people to submit to David.

That event pictured the way souls are brought into obedience to the Lord Jesus Christ.

Our earthly lives have little lasting substance.

It is strange that a soul destined to live forever devotes so many of its concerns to a body that will soon die.

Life passes like a moving shadow.

Even when believers enjoy great honor, they should remember their own unworthiness and sin, so that they are protected from pride and self-importance.

The Lord often comes to help his people when they are sinking and every other source of help has failed.

Praying for families, peace and the Lord's rule (verses 9–15)

New mercies call for new thanksgiving.

Praise God not only for what he has already granted, but also for the good he has promised and we still hope to receive.

Physical deliverance, whether from a sword or from wasting disease, would be of little ultimate value if a person remained under sin's dominion and the judgment to come.

David therefore prayed for his kingdom's prosperity.

Parents find joy in seeing their children likely to grow and do well.

May they be like healthy plants, not weeds or thorns.

May they grow rather than wither, bear fruit for God in their generation and become strong in the Spirit while young.

It is right to desire prosperity and full storehouses if these gifts make us more thankful toward God, generous to friends and charitable to poor people.

If our abundance produces none of these things, what profit is there in it?

We should also desire peace.

War causes countless harms, whether a people are attacking others or defending themselves.

A nation's real happiness declines as its people neglect God's worship and service.

Those who belong to the Savior, the Son of David, share the blessings of his kingdom and victories.

They are happy because the Lord is their God.
classic_reading:
[Ps.144.1-Ps.144.8]
Chapter 144
Chapter Outline
David acknowledges the great goodness of God, and prays for help. | (1-8) |
He prays for the prosperity of his kingdom. | (9-15) |
Verses 1-8
When men become eminent for things as to which they have had few advantages, they should be more deeply sensible that God has been their Teacher. Happy those to whom the Lord gives that noblest victory, conquest and dominion over their own spirits. A prayer for further mercy is fitly begun with a thanksgiving for former mercy. There was a special power of God, inclining the people of Israel to be subject to David; it was typical of the bringing souls into subjection to the Lord Jesus. Man's days have little substance, considering how many thoughts and cares of a never-dying soul are employed about a poor dying body. Man's life is as a shadow that passes away. In their highest earthly exaltation, believers will recollect how mean, sinful, and vile they are in themselves; thus they will be preserved from self-importance and presumption. God's time to help his people is, when they are sinking, and all other helps fail.
[Ps.144.9-Ps.144.15]
Verses 9-15
Fresh favours call for fresh returns of thanks; we must praise God for the mercies we hope for by his promise, as well as those we have received by his providence. To be saved from the hurtful sword, or from wasting sickness, without deliverance from the dominion of sin and the wrath to come, is but a small advantage. The public prosperity David desired for his people, is stated. It adds much to the comfort and happiness of parents in this world, to see their children likely to do well. To see them as plants, not as weeds, not as thorns; to see them as plants growing, not withered and blasted; to see them likely to bring forth fruit unto God in their day; to see them in their youth growing strong in the Spirit. Plenty is to be desired, that we may be thankful to God, generous to our friends, and charitable to the poor; otherwise, what profit is it to have our garners full? Also, uninterrupted peace. War brings abundance of mischiefs, whether it be to attack others or to defend ourselves. And in proportion as we do not adhere to the worship and service of God, we cease to be a happy people. The subjects of the Saviour, the Son of David, share the blessings of his authority and victories, and are happy because they have the Lord for their God.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDavid extols the power, goodness, and mercy of the Lord.1–9The glory of God's kingdom, and his care of those that love him.10–21
Thanksgiving for the Redeemer's goodness (verses 1–9)

Those who pray earnestly through troubles and temptations will eventually have abundant reason to thank God.

Grateful praise is the true language of holy joy.

Above all, we should celebrate God's wonderful work of redemption as we speak of his greatness.

Neither Israel's rescues nor the punishment of sinners reveals God's justice as clearly to an enlightened mind as the cross of Jesus Christ.

Everything the Lord Jesus says and does is marked by goodness and grace.

He is full of compassion.

That is why he came into this world to save sinners.

During his earthly life, he showed mercy to both people's bodies and their souls.

He healed bodily sickness and taught them heavenly wisdom.

He is the merciful High Priest through whom God shows mercy to sinners.

The Lord's care and the glory of his kingdom (verses 10–21)

All God's works declare his praise.

He supplies the needs of every living creature.

Yet sinful human beings can be so dissatisfied that nothing God gives them seems enough.

The Lord does good to all humanity, while showing his people special care.

Many believers have come close to falling into sin or despair.

God has shown his goodness by preventing their fall or quickly restoring them through grace and comfort.

Everyone carrying the heavy burden of sin may come to Christ in faith.

He will relieve and raise them.

The Lord willingly hears and answers his people's prayers.

He is present everywhere, yet in a special way near to those who call upon him sincerely.

By faith he lives within their hearts, and they remain in him.

He comes near in every hour of need, so that those who call upon him in truth and sincerity may receive what they ask and find what they seek.

He has taught them to love his name and holy ways.

He will therefore deliver them from the destruction awaiting the unrepentant.

May we love his name, obey his ways and pray that all humanity will praise his holy name forever.
classic_reading:
[Ps.145.1-Ps.145.9]
Chapter 145
Chapter Outline
David extols the power, goodness, and mercy of the Lord. | (1-9) |
The glory of God's kingdom, and his care of those that love him. | (10-21) |
Verses 1-9
Those who, under troubles and temptations, abound in fervent prayer, shall in due season abound in grateful praise, which is the true language of holy joy. Especially we should speak of God's wondrous work of redemption, while we declare his greatness. For no deliverance of the Israelites, nor the punishment of sinners, so clearly proclaims the justice of God, as the cross of Christ exhibits it to the enlightened mind. It may be truly said of our Lord Jesus Christ, that his words are words of goodness and grace; his works are works of goodness and grace. He is full of compassion; hence he came into the world to save sinners. When on earth, he showed his compassion both to the bodies and souls of men, by healing the one, and making wise the other. He is of great mercy, a merciful High Priest, through whom God is merciful to sinners.
[Ps.145.10-Ps.145.21]
Verses 10-21
All God's works show forth his praises. He satisfies the desire of every living thing, except the unreasonable children of men, who are satisfied with nothing. He does good to all the children of men; his own people in a special manner. Many children of God, who have been ready to fall into sin, to fall into despair, have tasted his goodness in preventing their falls, or recovering them speedily by his graces and comforts. And with respect to all that are heavy laden under the burden of sin, if they come to Christ by faith, he will ease them, he will raise them. He is very ready to hear and answer the prayers of his people. He is present every where; but in a special way he is nigh to them, as he is not to others. He is in their hearts, and dwells there by faith, and they dwell in him. He is nigh to those that call upon him, to help them in all times of need. He will be nigh to them, that they may have what they ask, and find what they seek, if they call upon him in truth and sincerity. And having taught men to love his name and holy ways, he will save them from the destruction of the wicked. May we then love his name, and walk in his ways, while we desire that all flesh should bless his holy name for ever and ever.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesWhy we should not trust in men.1–4Why we should trust in God.5–10
Human help is short-lived (verses 1–4)

Those who delight in praising God now will praise him forever. What little value worldly pursuits have compared with that prospect!

There is one Son of Man in whom help never fails, who is also the Son of God. All other sons of men share fallen Adam's condition. Adam did not remain in his original honor; neither can any other human being guarantee lasting happiness.

God gave the earth to humanity, yet people constantly struggle over it. Eventually even the most powerful person owns nothing but the small piece of ground where the body is buried. On the day of death, all earthly plans perish. We should not make other people the ultimate ground of our hope.

The Lord's eternal help and kingdom (verses 5–10)

For this life we hope in God's providence, and for the next we hope in his grace.

The God of heaven became human in order to save us. He died upon the cross for our sins and was laid in the grave; nevertheless, his purposes of love did not end there. He rose again to fulfill them.

Christ's earthly miracles picture the saving works he continues to perform every day. He liberates prisoners from sin and Satan, opens the eyes of understanding, feeds people who hunger for salvation with the bread of life, and shows mercy to the poor in spirit, the helpless and the spiritually fatherless.

His kingdom continues forever. Let sinners turn to him and believers rejoice in him. Let us encourage one another to praise his name.
classic_reading:
[Ps.146.1-Ps.146.4]
Chapter 146
Chapter Outline
Why we should not trust in men. | (1-4) |
Why we should trust in God. | (5-10) |
Verses 1-4
If it is our delight to praise the Lord while we live, we shall certainly praise him to all eternity. With this glorious prospect before us, how low do worldly pursuits seem! There is a Son of man in whom there is help, even him who is also the Son of God, who will not fail those that trust in him. But all other sons of men are like the man from whom they sprung, who, being in honour, did not abide. God has given the earth to the children of men, but there is great striving about it. Yet, after a while, no part of the earth will be their own, except that in which their dead bodies are laid. And when man returns to his earth, in that very day all his plans and designs vanish and are gone: what then comes of expectations from him?
[Ps.146.5-Ps.146.10]
Verses 5-10
The psalmist encourages us to put confidence in God. We must hope in the providence of God for all we need as to this life, and in the grace of God for that which is to come. The God of heaven became a man that he might become our salvation. Though he died on the cross for our sins, and was laid in the grave, yet his thoughts of love to us did not perish; he rose again to fulfil them. When on earth, his miracles were examples of what he is still doing every day. He grants deliverance to captives bound in the chains of sin and Satan. He opens the eyes of the understanding. He feeds with the bread of life those who hunger for salvation; and he is the constant Friend of the poor in spirit, the helpless: with him poor sinners, that are as fatherless, find mercy; and his kingdom shall continue for ever. Then let sinners flee to him, and believers rejoice in him. And as the Lord shall reign for ever, let us stir up each other to praise his holy name.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe people of God are exhorted to praise him for his mercies and care.1–11For the salvation and prosperity of the church.12–20
God gathers, heals and provides (verses 1–11)

Praising God is work that carries its own reward. It is fitting for all rational creatures and especially for people bound to him by covenant.

He gathers outcast sinners through grace and brings them into his holy dwelling. Through the comfort of his Spirit, he heals the brokenhearted, speaks peace and assures them that their sins are pardoned.

Our knowledge quickly reaches its limits, but God's wisdom cannot be measured. He counts the stars and listens to the brokenhearted. He feeds young ravens; surely he will not neglect his praying people.

Clouds appear dark, yet without them there would be no rain or fruit. Likewise clouds of affliction can yield the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

God does not admire the outward powers and achievements in which sinners glory. He values sincere reverence and trust. Faithful people should act under the gracious influence of hope and fear joined together.

God's word and Spirit melt frozen hearts (verses 12–20)

God's wisdom, power and goodness build and preserve his church as they preserved Jerusalem. His blessings in nature picture his gracious work.

The word that makes winter ice melt can represent the gospel of Christ, while the thawing wind pictures the Spirit of Christ, whom Scripture compares to the wind (John 3:8).

Converting grace softens a heart that was frozen hard, melting it into tears of repentance and releasing good thoughts and affections once held back. The change brought about by the thaw is visible although its workings are mysterious. So is the transformation when God's word and Spirit bring a soul to repentance and life.
classic_reading:
[Ps.147.1-Ps.147.11]
Chapter 147
Chapter Outline
The people of God are exhorted to praise him for his mercies and care. | (1-11) |
For the salvation and prosperity of the church. | (12-20) |
Verses 1-11
Praising God is work that is its own wages. It is comely; it becomes us as reasonable creatures, much more as people in covenant with God. He gathers outcast sinners by his grace, and will bring them into his holy habitation. To those whom God heals with the consolations of his Spirit, he speaks peace, assures them their sins are pardoned. And for this, let others praise him also. Man's knowledge is soon ended; but God's knowledge is a dept that can never be fathomed. And while he telleth the number of the stars, he condescends to hear the broken-hearted sinner. While he feeds the young ravens, he will not leave his praying people destitute. Clouds look dull and melancholy, yet without them we could have no rain, therefore no fruit. Thus afflictions look black and unpleasant; but from clouds of affliction come showers that make the soul to yield the peaceable fruits of righteousness. The psalmist delights not in things wherein sinners trust and glory; but a serious and suitable regard to God is, in his sight, of very great price. We are not to be in doubt between hope and fear, but to act under the gracious influences of hope and fear united.
[Ps.147.12-Ps.147.20]
Verses 12-20
The church, like Jerusalem of old, built up and preserved by the wisdom, power, and goodness of God, is exhorted to praise him for all the benefits and blessings vouchsafed to her; and these are represented by his favours in the course of nature. The thawing word may represent the gospel of Christ, and the thawing wind the Spirit of Christ; for the Spirit is compared to the wind, [John.3.8] Joh 3:8. Converting grace softens the heart that was hard frozen, and melts it into tears of repentance, and makes good reflections to flow, which before were chilled and stopped up. The change which the thaw makes is very evident, yet how it is done no one can say. Such is the change wrought in the conversion of a soul, when God's word and Spirit are sent to melt it and restore it to itself.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe creatures placed in the upper world called on to praise the Lord.1–6Also the creatures of this lower world, especially his own people.7–14
The heavens praise their Creator (verses 1–6)

We know little of the heavenly world of light while living in this dark and sinful world. Yet we know that holy angels dwell there and continually praise God.

The psalmist calls them to praise him in the finest possible way. By joining them we acknowledge our fellowship with the spirits above.

The heavens and everything within them declare the Lord's glory. They call us to honor the Creator and Redeemer of the universe in both words and deeds.

Every creature and every person called to praise (verses 7–14)

God is praised even in a fallen world. Nature's strongest and stormiest forces do only what he directs. People who rebel against his word may seem more violent than storm winds, but they cannot thwart his purpose.

Mountains and hills, barren and fertile alike, give reasons for praise. Rational creatures should praise him especially, whatever their social position.

His saints should praise him continually. He is not only our Creator but our Redeemer, who has brought his people near.

Henry says that “the horn of his people” may mean Christ, whom God has exalted as Prince and Savior, the eternal defense and praise of his saints. Redemption displays extraordinary glory and supplies the foundation for our hope and joy.

May the Lord forgive us and teach us to love him more and praise him better.
classic_reading:
[Ps.148.1-Ps.148.6]
Chapter 148
Chapter Outline
The creatures placed in the upper world called on to praise the Lord. | (1-6) |
Also the creatures of this lower world, especially his own people. | (7-14) |
Verses 1-6
We, in this dark and sinful world, know little of the heavenly world of light. But we know that there is above us a world of blessed angels. They are always praising God, therefore the psalmist shows his desire that God may be praised in the best manner; also we show that we have communion with spirits above, who are still praising him. The heavens, with all contained in them, declare the glory of God. They call on us, that both by word and deed, we glorify with them the Creator and Redeemer of the universe.
[Ps.148.7-Ps.148.14]
Verses 7-14
Even in this world, dark and bad as it is, God is praised. The powers of nature, be they ever so strong, so stormy, do what God appoints them, and no more. Those that rebel against God's word, show themselves to be more violent than even the stormy winds, yet they fulfil it. View the surface of the earth, mountains and all hills; from the barren tops of some, and the fruitful tops of others, we may fetch matter for praise. And assuredly creatures which have the powers of reason, ought to employ themselves in praising God. Let all manner of persons praise God. Those of every rank, high and low. Let us show that we are his saints by praising his name continually. He is not only our Creator, but our Redeemer; who made us a people near unto him. We may by "the Horn of his people" understand Christ, whom God has exalted to be a Prince and a Saviour, who is indeed the defence and the praise of all his saints, and will be so for ever. In redemption, that unspeakable glory is displayed, which forms the source of all our hopes and joys. May the Lord pardon us, and teach our hearts to love him more and praise him better.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesJoy to all the people of God.1–5Terror to their enemies.6–9
A new song for the new creation (verses 1–5)

New mercies call for new songs of praise, on earth and in heaven.

The children of Zion should thank God for creating them, but also for making them new creations in Christ Jesus for good works. They were not merely made human; he formed them as saints.

The Lord takes pleasure in his people; they should delight in him.

When sinners feel their need and unworthiness, God clothes them with the graces of his Spirit and restores his image within them. Their joy will continue forever.

Let believers sing even during wakeful nights. On their deathbeds, they can rejoice in the hope of eternal rest and glory.

Christ's victory is not spread by human violence (verses 6–9)

Certain servants of God in ancient times were specifically appointed to carry out his judgments, not from private revenge or political ambition, but in obedience to a particular command.

But the victory promised to all God's saints concerns the enemies of their salvation.

Christ did not intend his gospel to be spread by fire and sword, nor his righteousness by human wrath.

Instead, let his praises be in our mouths and the sword of the word of God in our hands, with the shield of faith as we struggle against the world, the flesh and the devil.

Through the blood of the Lamb and his testimony, believers will become more than conquerors. Final judgment will be carried out on the great day.

Henry also asks us to picture Christ and his gospel church, especially in what he calls her millennial condition.

Christ and his people rejoice in one another. Through their prayers and efforts, they work with him as he advances in the chariots of salvation, conquering sinners by grace, or in chariots of vengeance, bringing destruction upon his enemies.

Chapter 149
Chapter Outline
Joy to all the people of God. | (1-5) |
Terror to their enemies. | (6-9) |
Verses 1-5
New mercies continually demand new songs of praise, upon earth and in heaven. And the children of Zion have not only to bless the God who made them, but to rejoice in him, as having created them in Christ Jesus unto good works, and formed them saints as well as men. The Lord takes pleasure in his people; they should rejoice in Him. When the Lord has made sinners feel their wants and unworthiness, he will adorn them with the graces of his Spirit, and cause them to bear his image, and rejoice in his happiness for ever. Let his saints employ their waking hours upon their beds in songs of praise. Let them rejoice, even upon the bed of death, assured that they are going to eternal rest and glory.
[Ps.149.6-Ps.149.9]
Verses 6-9
Some of God's servants of old were appointed to execute vengeance according to his word. They did not do it from personal revenge or earthly politics, but in obedience to God's command. And the honour intended for all the saints of God, consists in their triumphs over the enemies of their salvation. Christ never intended his gospel should be spread by fire and sword, or his righteousness by the wrath of man. But let the high praises of God be in our mouths, while we wield the sword of the word of God, with the shield of faith, in warfare with the world, the flesh, and the devil. The saints shall be more than conquerors over the enemies of their souls, through the blood of the Lamb and the word of his testimony. The completing of this will be in the judgement of the great day. Then shall the judgement be executed. Behold Jesus, and his gospel church, chiefly in her millennial state. He and his people rejoice in each other; by their prayers and efforts they work with him, while he goes forth in the chariots of salvation, conquering sinners by grace, or in chariots of vengeance, to destroy his enemies.

modern_osis:
Original heading

A psalm of praise.

Everything that breathes, praise the Lord

We are summoned to praise God in his sanctuary and for the privilege of worshiping him.

The heavens display his power and glory in ways that their blessed inhabitants see far more fully than we do.

Yet his greatest mighty work has been revealed in his earthly sanctuary: the redemption of human beings.

God's holiness and love shine more clearly in redemption than in all his other works.

We should therefore praise our God and Savior.

The precise names of the musical instruments are not the heart of the passage. What matters is that we spare no effort or expense in serving God.

Praise him with strong faith.

Praise him through holy love and delight.

Praise him with complete confidence in Christ.

Praise him in believing triumph over the powers of darkness.

Praise him through obedience to every command.

Praise him with cheerful submission to all his appointments.

Praise him by rejoicing in his love and taking comfort in his goodness.

Praise him by promoting the interests of the kingdom of grace.

Praise him with hope in the kingdom of his glory.

Soon each of us will draw a final breath. Therefore, while we still have breath, let us praise the Lord, so that even death may find us full of comfort.

Let everything that breathes praise the Lord. Praise the Lord!

This is a fitting conclusion to the book of Psalms, inspired by the Spirit and written for praise.

Henry emphasizes that it has provided songs for God's people for more than three thousand years, and he calls it the book most frequently quoted by Christ and his apostles.

It speaks of God's majesty and government, addresses every human condition and every sort of spiritual experience, and displays clear marks of divine inspiration.
classic_reading:
[Ps.150.1]
Chapter 150
A psalm of praise.
--We are here stirred up to praise God. Praise God for his sanctuary, and the privileges we enjoy by having it among us; praise him because of his power and glory in the firmament. Those who praise the Lord in heaven, behold displays of his power and glory which we cannot now conceive. But the greatest of all his mighty acts is known in his earthly sanctuary. The holiness and the love of our God are more displayed in man's redemption, than in all his other works. Let us praise our God and Saviour for it. We need not care to know what instruments of music are mentioned. Hereby is meant that in serving God we should spare no cost or pains. Praise God with strong faith; praise him with holy love and delight; praise him with entire confidence in Christ; praise him with believing triumph over the powers of darkness; praise him by universal respect to all his commands; praise him by cheerful submission to all his disposals; praise him by rejoicing in his love, and comforting ourselves in his goodness; praise him by promoting the interests of the kingdom of his grace; praise him by lively hope and expectation of the kingdom of his glory. Since we must shortly breathe our last, while we have breath let us praise the Lord; then we shall breathe our last with comfort. Let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord. Praise ye the Lord. Such is the very suitable end of a book inspired by the Spirit of God, written for the work of praise; a book which has supplied the songs of the church for more than three thousand years; a book which is quoted more frequently than any other by Christ and his apostles; a book which presents the loftiest ideas of God and his government, which is fitted to every state of human life, which sets forth every state of religious experience, and which bears simple and clear marks of its Divine origin.
